name: Blue Bell
lede: Blue Bell is a pale, dusty violet-blue; its name could point to the flower, to a famous jeans maker or to a crayon, and no book we hold says which.

sections.title: Three Blue Bells
sections.body:
The flower comes first. Paterson defines bluebell as the blue of the plant with blue bell-shaped flowers, also called wood hyacinth [1]. Baty's table of Werner's colors lists a Spanish bluebell among its flowers, so the plant appears in the old color-naming tradition [2].

The second is a company. Pastoureau notes that Blue Bell, which became Wrangler in 1947, offered Levi's the stiffest competition in jeans from 1919 [3]. The third is a crayon: the library records that Wikipedia attributes the name to Crayola [4]. The swatch itself is recorded in Maerz and Paul (1930) as first used in 1920, plate 37 J 10, and in ISCC-NBS block 182 [4]. None of the books connects the swatch to any of the three, so the origin is undocumented [1][2][3][4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is pale and greyed: lightness 68, chroma 25, hue angle 293 [4]. Its nearest plain name is [[periwinkle]], 6.0 units away, and [[lavender-blue]], [[lavender]] and [[wisteria]] stand beside it [4]. Next to a real flower it will look duller, since a page of aged paint is not a petal [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The hue is present in 28 of 23,781 paintings (0.12 per cent), rarer than 63 per cent of the named colors, and in a painting it is most often an accent [5]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 10 of 8,345 paintings, 1.6 times the baseline [5]. The painter most devoted to it is [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]], in 5 of 287 works here, 5.9 times the baseline, and it is over-represented in American paintings, 4.1 times, with 8 of 1,729 [5].

The earliest match dates to 1425, a Botticelli, 505 years before the name's record in 1930 [4][5]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a bluebell test [5]. In Google Books the words *blue bell* peak in the 1980s, but they count every sense, including brands and places, so the curve does not describe the color [6].

origin.named_after: undocumented; the bluebell flower is the likeliest sense

questions.q: What did the Blue Bell jeans company become in 1947?
The books we hold document the origin of the color name Blue Bell.

openers: Blue Bell can mean a flower, a jeans maker or a crayon, and no book picks one.
Sargent uses this dusty violet-blue 5.9 times more than expected.

issues: Baty pairing of Spanish bluebell with Indigo Blue was not clearly supported by the garbled table; reduced to a listing.
